title: Crisafulli government banks on repurposing $150,000 slogan
full_text:
The cash-strapped Queensland government has shelled out $150,000 to buy the trademark for the decades-old bank slogan “You can count on a Queenslander” to rebrand the state’s disaster recovery efforts.
Government spending disclosures and Intellectual Property Australia records show David Crisafulli’s Department of Premier and Cabinet spent $150,000 of taxpayer cash to snag the exclusive use of the nostalgic Bank of Queensland phrase from private company Queensland Brand Partners Pty Ltd.
The Australian understands the Liberal National Party government plans to use the slogan for a disaster recovery website and for Queensland Day awards, and has already “soft-launched” the phrase in a very limited way.
IP Australia records show the state has trademarked the slogan for marketing, printed publications, clothing, carrying bags, kitchen utensils and stubby coolers, beer and non-alcoholic beverages, and vehicle number plates.
There is a stated condition that “the trademark will only be used in respect of beer produced in Queensland”.
On the state’s official disaster website, there is a maroon “You can count on a Queenslander” logo, along with the statement “when disaster strikes, you can count on a Queenslander” in a section that deals with post-disaster financial help, replacing lost documents, rebuilding and cleaning up, and seeking legal help.
A spokesman for Mr Crisafulli said the phrase “will be used to encourage volunteerism and donations during disasters”; he did not say whether the slogan had been market-tested before it was bought. Bank of Queensland let its trademark of the slogan lapse in the 1990s.
The Queensland government’s pre-disaster slogan is “Get Ready Queensland”, which was trademarked by the Queensland Reconstruction Authority in May 2020. It’s not clear how much that slogan cost to buy or develop.
Political advertising experts have questioned whether the $150,000 trademark purchase represented good value for money for taxpayers.
Toby Ralph, a marketer and researcher specialising in persuasion, who has worked on more than 50 elections globally including John Howard’s campaigns, said at “$25,000-a-word” it “sounds like a government shopping expedition” for a “recycled slogan”.
“Somewhere there’s a taxpayer wondering whether they could’ve fixed a few potholes instead. I’d have knocked one up for $145,000,” Mr Ralph joked.
“Governments and corporates have an unhealthy habit of believing that changing the slogan changes reality. It doesn’t. If the roads are bad and the hospitals are full, no slogan fixes that. Buying nostalgia is easy. Delivering competent government is considerably harder. Good advertising starts with an insight, not a slogan,” he said. “ The slogan can help, but it can’t do the heavy lifting. The danger is confusing brand recognition with brand affection. People remember plenty of slogans. They don’t necessarily believe them. If the slogan worked because people trusted the old bank, the government still has to earn that trust itself. You can’t buy credibility at the intellectual property office. Marketing can polish the silver, but it can’t convince people the cutlery drawer isn’t empty.
“Compared with most government spending, $150,000 is loose change down the back of the ministerial sofa. The real question isn’t whether they bought the slogan, it’s whether they can live up to it.” Campaign Edge founding partner Dee Madigan, who has worked on advertising for Queensland and federal Labor election campaigns, said she hoped the government had market-tested the phrase before spending $150,000.
“You should never spend six figures on IP without testing whether it still means anything,” said Ms Madigan, the lead creative on federal Labor’s 2022 and 2025 election victories. “But I’d be surprised if it tested well enough to spend that sort of money. Everyone over 50 remembers it as a bank ad. Everyone under 40 has never heard it.
“So they’ve paid $150,000 for nostalgia that half the market doesn’t have, attached to brand equity that belongs to a bank, and even the bank decided it wasn’t worth keeping.
“So maybe you can count on a Queenslander but not on the Department of Premier and Cabinet to do a cost-benefit analysis first.” In the wake of the June budget, ratings agency S&P Global again warned the government about the state’s “very weak fiscal position” and said Queensland’s fiscal repair would “hinge on successful control of operating expenses over the next two years”.
The “you can count on a Queenslander” slogan was created for Bank of Queensland by advertising executive Greville Patterson in the late 1970s when he was working as art director for the Brisbane branch of US advertising agency Ogilvy and Mather. The resulting ad jingle was sung by Doug Parkinson and TV commercials featured Queensland institutions such as cricketer Allan Border and brewery XXXX.
